one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban restates his death-penalty abolition position, occasioned by Mary Jane Veloso's reprieve in Indonesia. Our people are united in sympathizing with and helping Veloso, the poor Filipino female domestic worker convicted of heroin smuggling in Indonesia despite her defense that she was merely duped into carrying the prohibited drug in her suitcase; she was nonetheless sentenced to death in October 2010. Due to a moratorium then in effect, the sentence was not carried out immediately, but newly-elected Indonesian President Joko Widodo lifted the moratorium and she was scheduled for execution by firing squad on the evening of April 29 this year together with eight others. At the last moment, Widodo -- heeding P-Noy's plea -- granted her a reprieve so she could testify at the trial in the Philippines of her alleged recruiters, Maria Cristina Sergio and Sergio's live-in partner Julius Lacanilao. The other eight convicts were executed despite ringing protests of many world leaders. Veloso's heart-wrenching story reminds CJ of 'the grim finality of death as a penalty.' According to Amnesty International, the death penalty has been outlawed in 140 countries as an inhuman and ineffective deterrent. Our 1987 Constitution has also barred the imposition of the death penalty 'unless for compelling reasons involving heinous crimes, the Congress hereafter provides for it,' and the Charter reduced death sentences already imposed to reclusion perpetua. Citing the constitutional exception, Congress enacted RA 7659 prescribing death for certain crimes it defined as 'heinous.' In People v. Echegaray (June 25, 1996 and Feb 7, 1997), the SC upheld the constitutionality of RA 7659, adjudged Echegaray guilty of raping a 10-year-old girl, and meted out the death penalty by lethal injection -- the first under RA 7659. Together with two other justices, CJ dissented from this and all other judgments imposing death on the ground that RA 7659 was unconstitutional because Congress failed (1) to show 'compelling reasons' to revive death and (2) the crimes for which it was prescribed were not 'heinous.' Apart from these legal grounds, CJ also strongly felt the death penalty unfairly targeted the poor, the weak, and the underprivileged; though many decisions were per curiam, he has on many occasions admitted his dissenting opinions and votes. To help Mary Jane and her family escape the agony of firing-squad death, he revisits his arguments. The death penalty militates against 'the poor, the powerless and the marginalized.' The best example: Echegaray's counsel -- like Mary Jane's -- was 'less than competent and enthusiastic' in defending him; the crucial constitutionality issue was not raised in the trial court, not even in the SC, until Echegaray's counsel was replaced by the Free Legal Assistance Group, which belatedly brought it up only in the Supplemental MR. To the poor and unlettered, complex law in strange incomprehensible language and intimidating judicial proceedings engender 'unfounded at times, but unhealthy nevertheless ... a sense of the unequal balance of the scales of justice.' Precisely because the underprivileged are what they are, they require and deserve a greater degree of protection from Constitution, laws, officials, and courts so that, in spite of their situation, they can be empowered to rise above themselves and their poverty. The basic postulate is that ultimately we all want to better ourselves and cannot do so individually to a significant degree if we are unable to advance as an entire people and nation. All the glory provisions of the Constitution aim to help the poor -- yet we were faced with a penalty that effectively inflicted the ultimate punishment on the poor and disadvantaged, so obviously final and irreversibly permanent that it erased all hopes of reform, of change for the better. After a long battle in courts of law and public opinion, Congress finally repealed the Death Penalty Law effective June 30, 2006. Had Congress not abolished it, P-Noy (and others who labored for Mary Jane) would not have had the 'moral ascendancy' to plead for her life. This is one more reason why the death penalty should remain dead -- in deference to and for the sake of our poor, struggling OFWs, many of whom are virtually and unfairly lined up before firing squads in many countries of the world.
